name: PT Chandra Asri Pacific Tbk

frontmatter.title: Chandra Asri Pacific: a refinery-sized platform, a trough-sized margin
frontmatter.summary: Chandra Asri has become an integrated energy, chemicals and infrastructure group through the Aster refinery and Esso retail deals, but the enlarged platform earns a thin commodity spread and carries heavy debt. On our through-cycle DCF the shares trade below fundamental value; the konglo lens keeps only part of that discount for twelve months. Initiate ADD.
thesis: The enlarged platform is real: FY2025 revenue reached US$7,000.0m and H1-2026 revenue US$5,348.8m after the Aster refinery and Esso retail acquisitions, with management reporting record operating EBITDA of US$802.6m for the half [S5, S2, S6].

Reported FY2025 profit is not operating profit: it contains a US$1,772.2m pre-tax bargain-purchase gain on Aster, larger than the full-year attributable profit, so the headline net profit overstates earning power and the LTM multiples built on it are unusable [S2, S6].
The balance sheet carries the expansion: the debt raised for the refinery and retail deals, and finance costs of US$187.9m in the half, absorb a large share of operating profit [S2].

Our through-cycle DCF puts fundamental value at Rp1,579 a share against a Rp1,500 price; the price implies long-run revenue growth of 2.4%, so the market has not yet credited the recovery we forecast [S0].
The konglo lens sets the twelve-month target: at 0.87x fundamental value today the base regime case closes 30.0% of the log gap, giving Rp1,785 and a 19.7% return [S0].

catalysts.event: Nine-month 2026 results, the new buyback period and any update on the CA-EDC Phase II plan
First full quarter with the Esso retail network consolidated
First free-float compliance deadline under the OJK fifteen per cent rule
MSCI consultation feedback closes; decision on Standalone status due by mid-2027
CA-EDC chlor-alkali and EDC plant scheduled start-up

blocks.text: We initiate PT Chandra Asri Pacific at ADD with a twelve-month target of Rp1,785 against a last price of Rp1,500, a return of 19.7%. The fundamental twelve-month value is Rp1,965; the konglo lens sets the target below it because the shares already trade at 0.87x our fundamental value today of Rp1,717.9, a discount, and the base regime case closes only 30.0% of the log gap within the year [S0].

The company is no longer the domestic olefins producer the name used to describe. The Aster acquisition, the former Shell energy and chemicals park in Singapore bought with Glencore, turned it into an integrated refinery and petrochemical group, and the Esso retail network bought from ExxonMobil completed on the first day of 2026 [S4, S5]. Revenue for FY2025 was US$7,000.0m and H1-2026 revenue was US$5,348.8m, more than four-fifths higher year on year [S5, S2, S6]. Management calls the half's operating EBITDA of US$802.6m a record and the first clean read on the enlarged platform [S6].

The variant view is about what that profit is. FY2025 net profit of US$1,090.1m looks spectacular against a FY2024 loss, but H1-2025 carries a US$1,772.2m pre-tax bargain-purchase gain on Aster, larger than the full-year attributable profit, so the headline flatters earning power [S5, S2]. Strip the gain out and the enlarged group earned very little in its first year: the pack's FY2025 EBITDA is US$-389.2m [S0]. The H1-2026 recovery to US$802.6m of operating EBITDA is the number that matters, but on the LK's own lines selling, G&A and the final tax leave a lower operating figure and management's definition adds back the other loss and the associates' profit [S2, S6]. Our forecast does not extrapolate the record half.

What moves the value. First, the petrochemical spread: our DCF is a through-cycle valuation and the single largest sensitivity is the gross margin, not volume. Second, the Brent deck: naphtha and refinery crude are the cost base, and because our calibrated link passes only four-fifths of a feedstock move into product prices, a higher oil deck compresses the margin mechanically [S2]. For an integrated refinery that link is a simplification: the record H1-2026 half was earned at a higher Brent than FY2025, so product cracks and refinery runs can offset the feedstock squeeze, and the model carries only the cost side of that tilt. Third, the balance sheet: net debt of US$2,898.5m at 2.3x forecast EBITDA is high, but the modelled path deleverages to US$1,800.4m by FY2028E as CA-EDC starts and capex steps down [S2, S5].

The price has not yet credited the recovery. On our reverse DCF the market is discounting long-run revenue growth of 2.4%, close to the three per cent we forecast, which is why the through-cycle DCF value of Rp1,579 sits above the Rp1,500 price [S0]. We are not calling the cycle turned; we are saying the through-cycle value is no longer reflected in the price after the platform transformation, and the twelve-month lens captures only part of the gap.

Chandra Asri Pacific is the listed chemicals and energy arm of the Barito Pacific group, controlled by Prajogo Pangestu. The group's own accounts describe it as belonging to the Barito Pacific group and put its factories in Cilegon and Puloampel, Banten, with the head office in the Wisma Barito Pacific tower in Jakarta [S2]. The company reports three strategic pillars, energy, chemicals and infrastructure, and the infrastructure pillar is the separately listed PT Chandra Daya Investasi, in which TPIA holds a direct sixty per cent stake [S5, S2].

The chemicals pillar is the original business: an integrated naphtha cracker producing olefins such as ethylene and propylene, and polyolefins sold as polyethylene and polypropylene, plus styrene monomer, butadiene and other derivatives. The refinery pillar is the transformed part. The Aster complex, formerly the Shell energy and chemicals park in Singapore, was acquired with Glencore and is consolidated as Aster Chemicals and Energy; it contributes refinery products and petrochemicals and is the main reason revenue multiplied [S4, S5]. The downstream portfolio was extended with the acquisition of Chevron Phillips Singapore Chemicals, now Aster Polymer Solutions, which adds 400 ktpa of high-density polyethylene capacity and a wider regional marketing footprint [S5].

The infrastructure pillar, CDIA, runs electricity, water, port and storage, and logistics assets serving the same industrial estate. Management reports a fleet of fourteen gas and chemical vessels and more than two hundred trucks, and a port and storage concession from the transport ministry [S5]. We value the consolidated group and deduct the minority interests, which include the forty per cent of CDIA that TPIA does not own [S2, F14]. We do not mark CDIA at its market price anywhere in this note; the bridge re-marks that forty per cent from its book carrying value to our published CDIA fundamental value, and deliberately not to the CDIA twelve-month target or market price, both of which contain a premium our own CDIA work rejects [S2, F14].

The domestic project pipeline is the growth story management sells. The chlor-alkali and ethylene dichloride project, known as CA-EDC, is a US$800.0m investment that management says was more than half complete at the FY2025 results and remains on track to start in the first quarter of 2027; Danantara and the Indonesia Investment Authority are co-investing in it [S5]. Management is also preparing a second phase of the project at a similar size; it is at the preparation stage, so it is a monitoring item rather than a committed cash flow in our capex path [S6]. The project is designed to feed the domestic alumina and mining chain and to reduce import dependence, which is why it has state backing [S5].

The group employed 4,277 people at the end of June 2026, up from a smaller base at end-2025, reflecting the enlarged footprint [S2]. Its customers are converters and industrial buyers in Indonesia and, increasingly, in Singapore, China and Australia through the Aster marketing network [S5].

Petrochemical crackers are price-takers on both sides: naphtha is priced off oil and polymers are priced off regional supply and demand, so the operator's job is to run a low-cost, reliable plant and to integrate downstream. Refinery and petrochemical integration helps because the refinery can flex its product slate toward whichever margin is open. This is general industry logic, not a sourced fact about TPIA.

The industry is Asian petrochemicals in a supply-driven downcycle: management describes the petrochemical market as still challenging [S6], Chinese and Middle Eastern capacity additions have pushed polymer and olefin spreads toward cash cost, and older naphtha crackers in Japan and Korea have been closing. The market is large and cyclically priced; nobody sets the price, and the marginal producer's cash cost is the anchor. Our sector work therefore values the name on a through-cycle spread rather than on the current quarter, and treats the spot oil tape as a timing input, not a value input.

The cost curve runs through oil. Naphtha is the feedstock for the Indonesian cracker and crude is the feedstock for the Singapore refinery, so the group's cost base moves with Brent. The house oil deck has Brent at 96 for FY2026E, 84 for FY2027E and a long-run anchor of 75, against a FY2025 average of 68; spot is 110, well above the anchor, so the cycle position is a timing input rather than a value input. That path matters twice over: it raises feedstock cost, and because product prices lag and pass through only partially, it squeezes the spread before it widens again as oil mean-reverts. For an integrated refinery the sign is not one-way: in H1-2026, earned at a higher Brent than FY2025, gross margin was materially better than in the comparative half, because refinery cracks widened alongside the feedstock move [S2]. We carry only the cost side of that tilt, which is why the through-cycle value is not lifted by the current oil spike.

Regulation cuts both ways. The Indonesian state is actively supporting downstream chemicals capacity: Danantara and INA are co-investing in CA-EDC, and the project is framed as import substitution for the alumina and mining chain [S5]. That is a genuine tailwind for the chemicals pillar. Against it, the equity market regime for concentrated-ownership names has tightened sharply, which we treat in section six rather than here.

Competitive position. Chandra Asri is the incumbent domestic olefins producer and one of the few integrated refinery-plus-cracker operators in the region after the Aster deal. Its moat is integration and scale rather than cost leadership: the Singapore refinery gives feedstock flexibility and the domestic cracker gives local market access, but neither is a durable cost advantage against a Middle East gas-based producer. Our cost-curve read is that the integrated complex sits in the middle of the Asian cost curve, not in the first quartile, so it survives a normal trough but not a prolonged one without balance-sheet stress. That placement is our judgment, not a disclosure: the LK carries no cost-curve data, and we place the group mid-curve because its naphtha cracker and Singapore refinery compete on feedstock against Middle East gas-based units, not because of a published quartile [S2]. The CA-EDC project, if it starts on time, adds a protected domestic position in caustic soda and EDC, which is a more defensible margin than commodity polymers [S5].

Five forces, read across the pillars. Supplier power is high: naphtha and crude are globally priced and the group cannot influence them. Buyer power is high in commodity polymers, where converters can source from China or the Middle East, and lower in EDC and caustic where the domestic alternative is an import. Rivalry is high and rising in polymers; it is moderate in refinery products, where Singapore is a regional pricing hub. Substitutes are a slow threat in plastics recycling and a faster one in the energy transition. Entry barriers are capital and permitting, which is exactly why the state is a co-investor in the new plant [S5].

Market share is not disclosed in a form we can source. We can say the group is the largest domestic olefins producer by capacity, but we have no published share figure for the enlarged regional platform, and we flag that as a gap rather than invent one. Volume and utilisation by plant are also not disclosed in the interim accounts in a comparable series; the LK gives revenue and cost, not tonnes [S2]. That is thin evidence, and we say so.

The history is a story of two companies. FY2022 to FY2024 show the domestic chemical business in a trough: revenue fell from US$2,384.6m to US$1,785.4m and gross profit was barely positive in the best year [S0]. FY2025 is the transformation year, with revenue of US$7,000.0m as Aster consolidated from mid-year, but EBITDA of US$-389.2m because the acquired refinery ran at trough spreads and the pack's cost base carries the full-year depreciation of the enlarged asset base [S0]. The reported net profit of US$1,090.1m is therefore not comparable to anything before it: it is the one-off gain plus a small underlying result [S2, S5].

H1-2026 is the first clean operating half. Revenue was US$5,348.8m, raw materials and manufacturing US$4,455.5m, leaving a gross margin of sixteen point seven per cent; depreciation of US$164.1m sits below the gross-profit line as its own expense, and finance costs were US$187.9m [S2]. Management reports operating EBITDA of US$802.6m and net profit of US$283.2m attributable to shareholders [S6, S2]. That is a genuine improvement, and it is the anchor for our forecast.

Our forecast. Revenue grows 52.0% in FY2026E to US$10,640.0m, because the year contains a full twelve months of Aster and the first year of Esso retail, then three per cent a year as CA-EDC starts and volumes grow [S5]. After the oil link the effective FY2026E gross margin is lower than the base input margin, and the resulting EBITDA margin is 12.0% [S2, S6]. We are deliberately not extrapolating the record half.

Management's operating EBITDA is not an LK line. On the LK, revenue of US$5,348.8m less raw materials of US$4,455.5m leaves gross profit, from which selling of US$41.6m, G&A of US$91.3m and the final tax of US$3.3m take the operating result lower; management's US$802.6m adds back the US$39.1m other net loss and the associates' profit [S2, S6]. The half is therefore less strong than the headline definition implies, and we anchor on the LK-consistent figure rather than the management number.

Costs and margins. The opex ratio of six point two per cent is the full H1-2026 build: selling of US$41.6m, G&A of US$91.3m, final tax of US$3.3m, the other net loss of US$39.1m and depreciation of US$164.1m together are about six point two per cent of revenue, and adding back depreciation gives EBITDA [S2]. The other net loss alone is under one per cent of revenue and is carried inside the model's EBITDA drag; we keep it as a recurring conservative item and would let the margin rise if it reverses. We hold it flat in real terms. The cost link to Brent is a calibration, not a company disclosure: we set sixty per cent of the cost base as oil-linked and four-fifths of a feedstock move as passed into prices, giving a net twelve per cent cost exposure, because that pair reproduces the H1-2026 margin at that half's Brent [S2]. We tested the same pair against the H1-2025 comparative, where revenue of US$2,913.4m and raw materials of US$2,890.2m imply a near-zero gross margin, and against the FY2025 pack, which is also near zero [S2, S0]. Both are scope-broken because Aster consolidated only from mid-2025 and the acquisition accounting distorts the comparatives, so H1-2026 is the only clean observation; we state the pair as a calibration with that limitation rather than as a sourced parameter [S2].

Cash flow and capex. H1-2026 acquisitions of property, plant and equipment were US$283.8m, mainly the CA-EDC project and sustaining capital [S2]. We forecast capex at five point five per cent of revenue while CA-EDC completes, stepping down to four per cent thereafter, and we forecast free cash flow to the firm of US$39.1m in FY2026E as the working-capital build absorbs the revenue step-up. That first-year cash drag is the cost of carrying a much larger inventory and receivable book: inventories rose to US$2,237.9m from the prior year-end level with the Esso retail network, and operating cash flow was only US$9.6m in the half against management's EBITDA, so cash conversion was weak [S2]. We treat the working-capital build as a scope and seasonality effect, not a deterioration, but it is the central earnings-quality question and we watch the ratio of operating cash flow to EBITDA rather than a Sloan ratio computed on acquisition-distorted earnings [S2]. Management's preparation of CA-EDC Phase II at a similar size to Phase I is not in the capex path; we add it to the post-balance-sheet review and monitoring, not the base cash flows, until a final investment decision is announced [S6].

Balance sheet and debt. The forecast is rolled from the 30 June 2026 LK, not from stale annual balances: opening cash is the LK's US$2,739.8m at 31 December 2025 (the comparative column, excluding the other current financial assets), and opening debt carries the half-year drawdown to the LK's US$5,910.9m total at 30 June 2026 [S2]. On that base our FY2026E net debt is US$2,898.5m after interest, dividends and capex [S2, S0]. Net debt to EBITDA is 2.3x, high for a commodity business, but the modelled path deleverages to US$1,800.4m by FY2028E, about 1.1x EBITDA, and continues down as CA-EDC contributes and capex steps down [S0]. That path assumes the Danantara and Indonesia Investment Authority co-investment of the project equity funds the build, so the state partners' share does not add to TPIA's net debt; if they fund at the asset level, our consolidated treatment is neutral to the equity value because the minority absorbs its share [S5]. Cash is the LK's cash and cash equivalents; the further US$511.2m of other current financial assets (bonds, listed shares and credit-linked investments) is not treated as cash but carried in the bridge at a stated haircut [S2]. Finance costs of US$187.9m in the half are a real fixed claim on a business whose EBITDA is cyclical [S2].

Capital allocation. The company pays a small dividend, US$30.0m at the parent in H1-2026, and it buys back shares opportunistically: it ran a buyback from 19 October 2026 for up to about 800 million shares, then ended it early on 28 October and announced a new period with a different allocation [S2, S7, S0]. Because the replacement programme's size and term are undisclosed, we hold the share count flat rather than extrapolating the one-off reduction [S7]. The combination of a small dividend, a small buyback and heavy growth capex is consistent with a group that is still investing for scale rather than returning cash [S5].

Earnings-quality flags. The accruals picture is distorted by the acquisition, so we rely on the specific flags and on cash conversion rather than a Sloan ratio. First, the bargain-purchase gain of US$1,772.2m is a one-off and should never be capitalised; we exclude it from forecasts [S2]. Second, receivables and inventory both jumped with the Esso and Aster consolidation, and operating cash flow of US$9.6m against the LK-consistent EBITDA shows the working-capital drag; that is a scope and seasonality effect rather than a deterioration, but it is a real cash cost of the new group [S2]. Third, the reported profit is heavily minority-affected: TPIA owns 60 per cent of CDIA, leaving a forty per cent minority, and the Aster complex has external partners, so the share of profit attributable to minorities is material; the FY2025 total profit of US$1,400.0m is therefore not the attributable US$1,090.1m [S2]. Related-party trade is disclosed in the related-party note and small: related-party sales are 1.9% of revenue and related-party raw-material purchases 0.05% of raw-material purchases, so the leakage risk is in financing channels, not the trading book [S2]. We classify the first as a non-recurring item to strip out, and the rest as optics-class effects to disclose, not manipulation-class flags. Cash conversion, not the accrual ratio, is the KPI we monitor.

For a commodity chemical producer, the quality of earnings is mostly the quality of the spread: a profit earned in a tight market is real cash but not a durable margin, while a profit earned from a one-off acquisition gain is neither. The screens we run are designed to separate those two, which is why the bargain-purchase gain and the working-capital step dominate this section.

We value TPIA with the chemicals method set: a free-cash-flow-to-firm DCF at a through-cycle margin as the primary method, with EV/EBITDA and PE shown as unweighted cross-checks. The industry map's default is sixty per cent DCF, twenty-five per cent EV/EBITDA and fifteen per cent PE; we move to a full DCF weight because neither multiple has a usable metric this year. LTM EBITDA is negative in the transition year, so the EV/EBITDA leg would be a non-value carrying a quarter of the blend; LTM parent earnings carry the one-off bargain-purchase gain, so the PE leg capitalises an item we exclude everywhere else [S0, S2, F8]. The commodity-cyclical method card is explicit that a cyclical is never valued on current-year multiples, and a zero leg may not carry a method weight, so the through-cycle DCF is the only weighted method. The multiples stay in the table as context, not as value [S0].

The cost of capital is built from a risk-free rate of 5.0%, an equity risk premium plus country risk of 4.2% and 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 90.0% levered to 148.2% at the group's debt-to-equity, and a cost of debt of 7.0%. That gives a cost of equity of 15.0% and a WACC of 10.7% [S0]. The cost of debt is the normalised forward build, the risk-free rate plus the macro deck's average IDX corporate spread, not the LK's trailing cash cost of about six point four per cent on the 30 June debt, which is flattered by fixed-rate facilities signed before rates rose; the gap is the marginal refinancing cost [S2]. The high cost of equity is the honest price of a leveraged commodity business with a concentrated register, not a haircut we have added.

The DCF produces Rp1,579 a share, with the terminal value at 48.0% of the total, which is normal for a company whose cash flow recovers after the capex peak. The forecast holds the LK-consistent H1-2026 operating margin, lets revenue grow three per cent, and assumes terminal growth of two and a half per cent in dollars.

Cycle position and NAV at spot. The deck's spot Brent is 110 against a long-run anchor of 75, so the complex is at the high end of its range and the through-cycle marker, not the tape, is the value anchor. Marked at spot with no mean reversion, the calibrated oil link would hold the gross margin at or below the FY2026E forecast of 15.1% through the whole forecast instead of recovering to 16.8%; even the business-bear scenario, which cuts the margin by three points, values the equity at only Rp546 a share. NAV at spot is therefore below that bear value and far below the through-cycle Rp1,579: at today's oil tape the shares are not cheap, and the entire investment case rests on mean reversion to the deck anchor. That is the cycle-position statement the commodity-cyclical method card asks for, and it is why we value on the through-cycle marker rather than the spot tape.

The cross-checks are shown for context and carry no weight, and they are observed market multiples calculated from the Rp1,500 price and the engine's peer medians, not engine-computed valuation methods. On our FY2026E EBITDA the shares trade at 8.6x and on FY2027E at 7.0x against the peer-median multiple the engine derives; the LTM metric is negative, so the method cannot produce a value at all [S0]. The PE leg capitalises LTM parent earnings that include the bargain-purchase gain and would be negative without it, so it cannot anchor a through-cycle value [S0, S2]. Read together, the multiples say the market is paying a recovering multiple for a business with only one clean half behind it; they do not override the DCF. The fundamental value is therefore Rp1,965, the probability-weighted business-scenario value [S0].

The sensitivity grid makes the point that this is a spread business. A one percentage point change in the gross margin moves value more than a one percentage point change in WACC, and the oil deck enters through the same margin channel. We would rather be approximately right about the spread than precise about the discount rate.

What the price implies. A reverse DCF on the same model says the Rp1,500 price discounts long-run revenue growth of 2.4%, close to the three per cent we forecast [S0]. That does not look aggressive for a company with a new refinery and a new retail network, which is why we now find the through-cycle value above the price. It still means the margin of safety sits in the spread, not in the growth assumption.

The konglo lens. Price sits at 0.87x our fundamental value today of Rp1,717.9 — a discount, not a premium — and below the twelve-month fundamental value of Rp1,965 [S0]. The lens does not assume the gap closes within a year: the base regime case closes 30.0% of the log gap, the bear case adds -15.0% to it (a widening, not a closing) and the bull case closes 70.0%, so the target is Rp1,785, below the twelve-month fundamental value and above the price [S0]. Why is that the most likely path for this name? The float is thin at 25.4%, the stock has been deleted from the MSCI Global Standard index, and the marginal buyer is a flow investor rather than a fundamental one; the company is buying back stock, but the new programme's size is undisclosed [S11, S7]. The lens therefore assumes only part of the discount closes, not all of it.

Group consistency. TPIA owns sixty per cent of CDIA, which we cover separately [S2, F14]. We mark the forty per cent minority at our published CDIA house fundamental value, which is a SELL, and not at either the CDIA market price or the CDIA twelve-month target, both of which contain a konglo premium our own CDIA work rejects [S2, F14]. The consolidated DCF includes CDIA's cash flow in full and deducts the book minority; the bridge then adds back the difference between the book carrying value of that minority and its house fundamental mark, so the stake is carried at house value rather than at market [S2, F14]. We do not use the CDIA market price anywhere in this valuation.

The business scenarios are mirrored. The bear case cuts revenue growth by four points and the gross margin by three, which together describe a renewed Asian oversupply episode with oil high and pass-through weak; the bull case adds the same amounts and describes capacity closures, a strong refinery margin and an on-time CA-EDC start [S0]. The base case carries half the probability and holds the H1-2026 spread in real terms.

The regime scenarios are separate and are the ones the konglo lens runs. They are not our business scenarios: they map the premium or discount between price and fundamental value and close a share of the gap over twelve months depending on the regime flags [S0]. The base regime case closes 30.0% of the gap, the bear regime adds -15.0% to the log gap (widening it) and the bull regime closes 70.0% of it; with price today below fundamental value, the base and bull cases lift the target toward the twelve-month value while the bear case holds it near today's price, which is why the target sits between price and fundamental value even though the business scenarios are balanced [S0].
The downside risks, with likelihood and impact.

Regulatory and index risk, high likelihood, medium impact. The OJK has raised the minimum free float to fifteen per cent with a first deadline in March 2027, and MSCI has frozen index increases and opened a consultation on moving Indonesia to Standalone status, with feedback until April 2027 and a decision by mid-year [S8, S9]. A further index deletion or a Standalone decision would remove flow buyers from a thin register. TPIA has just been through one deletion; the risk is that the next one is the market classification itself [S9].

Commodity and spread risk, high likelihood, high impact. The company earns a commodity spread, and a renewed wave of Chinese capacity would compress it. This is the dominant sensitivity in the DCF and the reason the bear case is a spread case, not a volume case.

Macro and FX risk, medium likelihood, medium impact. Revenue is dollar-denominated and the shares are rupiah-denominated, so the rupiah matters for the share price even when it does not matter for the cash flow; the macro desk has the rupiah under balance-of-payments pressure [S0]. A weaker rupiah mechanically raises the rupiah value of a dollar DCF, which is a partial hedge, but it also raises imported input costs.

Operational risk, medium likelihood, high impact. A cracker or refinery outage at a single large site is a real earnings event; this is a business with concentrated physical assets. CA-EDC start-up slippage is the specific dated risk, because the project is the growth case and management has committed to the first quarter of 2027 [S5].

Liquidity and balance-sheet risk, medium likelihood, medium impact. Heavy debt against cyclical EBITDA and a free float of 25.4% means refinancing is a flow event as much as a credit event [S2]. The modelled path deleverages to US$1,800.4m by FY2028E as CA-EDC starts, and the group holds US$511.2m of current financial assets it could realise, so the risk is a trough-timing risk rather than an immediate solvency risk; a delay to CA-EDC or a second downcycle at current debt levels is what would force the issue [S0, S2]. The buyback shows the company can support the shares, but it also uses cash that could de-lever [S7].

Governance and group risk, medium likelihood, medium impact. The controller owns most of the company, the group has multiple listed vehicles, and related-party transactions are small but real: trade receivables from related parties are US$13.0m of the trade receivable book and trade payables to related parties are US$4.4m [S2]. The specific risk is that value is moved between group vehicles rather than earned in TPIA. On pledges, the interim LK cannot show controlling-share pledges; that disclosure lives in the annual report and the exchange's shareholding filings, so we withdraw the earlier checked-but-not-confirmed claim and list it as a gap to close at the next annual report [S2].

Signposts that would change our view. A sustained recovery in the polymer spread above our base, a CA-EDC start on time and on budget, and a free-float increase that restores index eligibility would all push us toward a more constructive rating. A renewed oversupply wave, a Standalone decision for Indonesia, or a leverage increase above our base would push the other way.

Commodity chemical equities usually bottom when the marginal producer is losing cash and capacity is closing, not when the headline profit recovers. The timing mismatch between price and earnings is why the method card insists on a through-cycle value rather than a spot multiple.

Ownership and control. TPIA belongs to the Barito Pacific group of Prajogo Pangestu; the accounts state that the company is part of the Barito Pacific group and its head office sits in the group's tower [S2]. The registry puts insider ownership at seventy-four per cent and the free float at 25.4%, above the new fifteen per cent minimum but concentrated enough that the controller sets the strategic agenda [S0, S8]. The group's listed perimeter includes CDIA, in which TPIA holds sixty per cent, and the group has been an active capital-markets issuer, which is the context for the stock's flow behaviour [S2]. Because the register is concentrated and the index regime has turned against it, the twelve-month price can sit away from fundamental value for longer than the business cycle; that is why the valuation applies the konglo lens, which assumes only part of today's discount closes in a year rather than erasing it [S0].

The 2026 regime. The exchange's concentrated-ownership framework, the free-float rule and MSCI's review are the three moving parts. The OJK rule raises the minimum free float from seven and a half to fifteen per cent, with a first deadline in March 2027 and a delisting path for companies that cannot comply [S8]. MSCI froze index increases for Indonesian securities, deletes names identified under the HSC framework, and on 15 October 2026 opened a consultation on reclassifying Indonesia to Standalone status, with feedback until 30 April 2027 and a decision by 30 June 2027 [S9]. TPIA was deleted from the MSCI Global Standard index at the May 2026 review [S11]. The company is not on the exchange's HSC list in the latest publication we have, so the deletion is an index-flow event rather than a finding of wrongdoing [S10]. On board status, the LK carries no exchange-board or special-notation disclosure and TPIA is absent from the late-October special-monitoring (HSC) publication, so we record the notation check as checked, none, and flag any formal board notation as a gap rather than a clean bill [S10].

Group transactions. The Aster acquisition was made with Glencore, and Sembcorp Utilities has announced a planned acquisition of twenty per cent of Aster Power, an Aster Chemicals and Energy joint-venture entity; the H1-2026 profit correction is explained by that planned transaction, not a completed sale [S6]. The Esso retail acquisition was financed with a KKR facility [S5]. These are large transactions that change the shape of the group and should be read together rather than in isolation. Related-party trade flows are disclosed in the related-party note: sales to related parties were 1.9% of revenue in H1-2026, raw-material purchases from related parties 0.05% of raw-material purchases and finished-goods purchases 0.06% of finished-goods purchases, with trade receivables from related parties of US$13.0m and trade payables to related parties of US$4.4m at 30 June 2026, small against the group's balance sheet [S2]. The intra-group financing channel is real — CDIA, sixty per cent owned, holds parent-issued equity-linked bonds and lends to CAP subsidiaries — and we treat it as a group funding arrangement to monitor rather than a leakage on the evidence available [S2, F14]. On pledges, the interim LK cannot show controlling-share pledges: that disclosure lives in the annual report and exchange shareholding filings, so we flag it as a gap rather than a clean bill [S2].

Auditor and reporting. The interim accounts are unaudited; the FY2025 figures are audited at the annual level. The LK is prepared in US dollars and presents depreciation as a separate line below gross profit, which is the main reconciliation difference against the data pack and the reason our margin build uses a six point two per cent opex ratio that includes depreciation [S2]. We have not sourced the auditor's opinion for the latest audited year and flag that as a gap.

Dividend record. The company pays a small dividend: US$30.0m at the parent in H1-2026, which is a low payout against reported profit because the reported profit is inflated by the one-off gain [S2, S0]. The dividend is not the anchor for this stock; the balance sheet and the capex cycle are.

ESG exposures. The material issues are carbon intensity at the refinery and cracker, process safety at a large integrated site, and water and waste management around the Cilegon estate. The company presents sustainability as one of its three pillars and has won external ESG awards, which we note but do not treat as evidence of a lower risk profile [S5]. The CA-EDC project is explicitly framed as part of the domestic energy-transition supply chain for alumina, which is a policy tailwind rather than an ESG improvement in itself [S5].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter and repeated here with the monitoring logic. The nine-month results, the new buyback terms and any update on the CA-EDC Phase II plan are the next hard data points; the buyback is small relative to the market cap but it tells us how the group is reading its own share price [S7, S6]. The Esso retail network's first full quarter is the first test of whether the downstream acquisition adds margin or just revenue [S5]. The free-float deadline in March 2027 is the first regulatory date that could force a structural change in the register [S8]. The MSCI consultation closes at the end of April 2027 and the decision is due by the end of June, which is the single largest regime catalyst for the name [S9]. CA-EDC start-up in the first quarter of 2027 is the operational catalyst that validates the growth case [S5].

Between updates we watch five KPIs, each tied to the model and to management's disclosure [S6, S2]. First, the quarterly gross margin, which is our spread proxy and the main driver of the DCF. Second, operating EBITDA against the LK-consistent definition, to see whether the run-rate holds as oil moves. Third, operating cash flow over EBITDA, because the working-capital build is the central quality question in the enlarged group. Fourth, net debt and interest cover against the modelled deleveraging path, because the balance sheet is the constraint on the bear case. Fifth, the free float and any index announcement, because the marginal price in this stock is set by flows rather than by the operating result.

We also watch the group's capital-markets activity, because the register and the perimeter are the group's levers [S2]. A rights issue, a placement, a spin-off or a further asset injection from the controller would change the share count and the per-share value, and the group has been an active issuer in these markets [S2]. The valuation holds the share count flat because the replacement buyback's size is undisclosed and it does not anticipate a large issuance; if one is announced, the model changes that day [S7].

For a thin-float conglomerate name, the calendar of index and regulatory events often matters more for the twelve-month price than the quarterly earnings. That is why the catalyst list leans on dates rather than on numbers.

bear.narrative: Chinese and Middle East capacity keeps polymer spreads compressed while a high Brent deck lifts naphtha with only partial pass-through; the refinery runs at mid-cycle, CA-EDC start-up slips, and the enlarged debt load keeps interest cover thin.

bull.narrative: Petrochemical spreads widen as older Asian crackers shut, the Singapore refinery captures a strong diesel and jet margin, CA-EDC starts on time into a protected domestic caustic and EDC market, and the balance sheet deleverages faster than assumed.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

groups.name: Barito group (Prajogo Pangestu)
groups.role: petrochemicals, refining and infrastructure; parent of CDIA (60%)

index_deletions.note: deleted at the May 2026 review; AMRT moved to Small Cap

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +52% is the first full year of Aster Chemicals and Energy (ex-Shell Singapore refinery, acquired with Glencore) plus the Esso retail network from 1 Jan 2026, which took FY2025 revenue to about US$7.0bn against H1-2026 revenue of US$5.35bn [S5, S2]; afterwards +3% a year from CA-EDC start-up in Q1 2027 and volume growth, not price [S5].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Calibration: H1-2026 gross margin of 16.7% (revenue US$5.35bn less raw materials and manufacturing US$4.46bn) was earned with Brent near US$85, above the FY2025 anchor of US$68.1 [S2]. Grossing it back through the calibrated oil link gives a 19.1% margin at base input costs; the gross-up is our calibration, not a disclosed figure, because FY2025 itself is a transition year with Aster consolidated only mid-year [S2, S0]. Held flat in real terms, no spread expansion assumed.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Calibration, not a company disclosure: we set 60% of COGS as oil-linked because naphtha and refinery crude dominate raw materials while utilities, labour and fixed manufacturing cost do not move with Brent [S2]. The pair split/pass is fitted on the only clean consolidated half, H1-2026, and tested against the FY2025 and H1-2025 comparatives below, which are scope-broken because Aster consolidated only from mid-2025 [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Calibration, not a company disclosure: with the 60% cost share, 80% pass-through gives a net 12% of COGS exposed to the Brent move, which is the pair that reproduces the 16.7% H1-2026 gross margin at that half's Brent and the 19.1% base margin at the FY2025 anchor [S2]. The H1-2026 half is the only clean scope; FY2025 and H1-2025 margins are distorted by the mid-2025 Aster consolidation and therefore cannot validate the pair [S2, S0].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: H1-2026 selling, G&A, final tax, other net loss and depreciation total US$332m on US$5,349m of revenue (6.2%); depreciation sits below the gross-profit line in this LK, so it is included here and added back to EBITDA [S2].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: H1-2026 depreciation of US$164.1m on US$5,348.8m revenue (3.07%); the pack's FY2025 D&A is close to the LK run-rate, so no restatement is needed [S2, S0].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: H1-2026 acquisitions of PP&E were US$283.8m (5.3% of revenue), running the US$800m CA-EDC project and sustaining the refinery and cracker; it steps down to 4% once CA-EDC completes in Q1 2027, converging on D&A plus growth [S2, S5].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Receivables US$844m plus inventory US$2,238m less payables US$1,710m equals US$1,372m, about 12.8% of annualised H1-2026 revenue; the Esso retail inventory step-up lifted it, and it should normalise toward the 8% FY2025 level [S2].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: H1-2026 income tax of US$62.8m on PBT of US$434.0m is 14.5%, reflecting final tax and incentives; we start at the observed 14.5% and step toward the 22% statutory rate by FY2029E as the mix normalises [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: H1-2026 finance costs of US$187.9m annualise to US$375.7m against US$5.91bn of debt at 30 Jun 2026, a 6.4% average cash cost including the refinery acquisition facilities [S2].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Recalibrated to the LK's cash and cash equivalents: H1-2026 finance income of US$60.8m annualises to US$121.7m on the LK cash of US$2,921.3m, a 4.2% yield; on the opening LK cash of US$2,739.8m this gives FY2026E interest income close to the earlier figure, so net income barely moves [S2].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E only: the LK's financing-liabilities reconciliation shows the total rising from US$5,414.2m at 1 January 2026 to US$5,910.9m at 30 June 2026, so the forecast is rolled from the balance-sheet-date debt of US$5,910.9m; the US$496.7m is the H1 drawdown already in the 30 Jun 2026 LK. Thereafter no new net debt: operating EBITDA and capex broadly fund interest and the small dividend [S2, S6, S7].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: the US$1.77bn Aster bargain-purchase gain in H1-2025 and the Sembcorp-related corrections are one-offs and are excluded from the forecast, though they remain in reported history [S2, S6].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: H1-2026 profit attributable to non-controlling interests was US$87.9m of US$371.2m (24%), driven by the 40% CDIA minority and the Glencore/Sembcorp interests in the Aster complex [S2].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The group paid US$30m of parent dividends in H1-2026 and US$50m in FY2025; the 10% payout reflects the modest DPS on the enlarged share count rather than a stated policy ratio [S2, S0].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Held flat: the October 2026 programme covered up to 0.92% of issued shares but was terminated early on 28 October 2026 and the replacement period has an undisclosed size and term, so a permanent annual shrinkage would be unsourced optimism [S7].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: US-dollar reporting: 2.5% nominal terminal growth, in line with long-run chemical volume growth plus dollar inflation, and below the Indonesian CPI deck because revenue is dollar-denominated [S5].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg is Rp0 with a 25% weight because LTM EBITDA is negative in a transition year, so a quarter of the method blend is a non-value. Applying the same engine peer median (5.93x) to FY2026E EBITDA of US$1,276.1m gives about Rp896/share; the blend rises from Rp1,162 to about Rp1,386 and the target from Rp1,627 to roughly Rp1,900+, which flips HOLD to BUY. The report itself shows the shares trade at 8.2x FY2026E EBITDA against that 5.9x peer median, so the forward multiple was available.
challenges.answer: Removed the zero-valued EV/EBITDA leg from the blend. The engine has no forward-multiple metric (ev_ebitda reads LTM only, which is negative in the transition year), so the documented reweight the challenge permits is used: weights go from the CHEMICALS default 60/25/15 to 100% through-cycle DCF, because neither multiple has a usable metric and the commodity-cyclical card forbids current-year multiples on a cyclical. The 25% zero leg is gone and the rating is ADD with the target at 1,785.

challenges.challenge: link1_share 0.60 and link1_pass 0.80 are key inputs presented as sourced from S2/S6. S2's only relevant disclosure (p.169) says revenue depends on naphtha and crude prices; it states no 60% cost share and no 80% pass-through, and S6 contains neither. The pair is a two-parameter back-solve on one clean half-year (it reproduces the 16.7% H1-2026 margin at Brent ~85) and drives FY2026E gross margin down from the 19.1% base to 15.12% and the whole DCF; the engine's own grid shows about Rp191/share per 1pp of gross margin.
challenges.answer: The 60% cost share and 80% pass-through are now presented explicitly as a calibration, not a company disclosure. The basis states the fitted pair and the net cost exposure, and the report tests the pair against the H1-2025 comparative (revenue F24, raw materials F25) and the FY2025 pack, showing both are scope-broken because Aster consolidated only from mid-2025, so H1-2026 is the only clean observation.

challenges.challenge: The report says the CDIA stake is "marked at our published CDIA house target, a SELL" and that a consolidated DCF plus a book-minority deduction is "the same economic treatment". No holdings block exists and the bridge deducts US$1,003.7m of book minority, of which CDIA's 40% is about US$704m. CDIA's own house fundamental is Rp83 today and Rp97 in twelve months, so 40% is US$226-266m; the Rp311 target, 40% of which is US$854m, itself contains CDIA's konglo premium, which must not enter TPIA's fundamental value. The claimed equivalence is false either way, worth roughly Rp100/share.
challenges.answer: Removed the false equivalence claim. Added a real holdings bridge item that re-marks the 40% CDIA minority from book to the CDIA house fundamental value today (not the premium-bearing target and not market), worth about Rp100 per TPIA share before other changes; the report now states the consolidated treatment plus bridge explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The oil link is one-sided: the model has no revenue-side oil term, so a higher Brent always squeezes the margin. For an integrated refinery-plus-petrochemical group, crude plus product cracks can widen margins, and the report's own record H1-2026 half was earned at Brent ~85 against 68.1 in FY2025, which contradicts a pure cost-squeeze sign. Oil spot is 110.62 against a 75 long-run anchor.
challenges.answer: Report now discloses that the model carries only the cost side of oil and that the record H1-2026 half was earned at a higher Brent with a materially better margin than H1-2025, so the refinery crack can reverse the sign; the cost-curve position is stated as mid-curve, not first quartile. The chunk is kept as a simplification because the engine template has no revenue-side oil term.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 says net debt at 1.9x "leaves little headroom", but the model deleverages to 1,323 in FY2028 (about 0.8x EBITDA) and to net cash by FY2035. Danantara and INA are co-investing US$200m of the US$800m CA-EDC (S5), which is not reflected in the capex or net-debt path, and the group holds US$511.2m of liquid financial assets. The balance-sheet risk is stated against the wrong path.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now states the modelled deleveraging path to FY2028E and beyond, notes the Danantara and INA project-equity co-investment is neutral to TPIA equity because the minority absorbs its share, and cites the liquid current financial assets; the wrong little-headroom framing is removed.

challenges.challenge: The base case anchors on management's "record operating EBITDA" of US$802.6m (15.0%), which is not reconciled to the LK. On S2, gross profit is 893.2 less selling 41.6, G&A 91.3 and final tax 3.3, leaving about US$757m (14.2%) before depreciation; management's figure adds back the US$39.1m other loss and US$7.2m share of associates. The half is therefore 6% less strong than the anchor implies, and the report never discloses the definition.
challenges.answer: Added the LK reconciliation using the LK lines: revenue F4 less raw materials F5, then selling F20, G&A F21 and final tax F22 leave a lower operating figure than management, whose F10 adds back the other loss F23 and associates. The calibration justification now uses the LK-consistent run-rate rather than the management figure.

challenges.challenge: The same S6 article reports "TPIA Siapkan Tahap II Proyek CA-EDC Senilai US$1 Miliar". A second US$1bn project is absent from the capex path (which steps down to 4.0% of revenue by FY2029), the post-balance-sheet review, the scenarios and the catalyst list. Against US$2.4bn of net debt and a base case with a US$13m first-year FCFF, that commitment is material.
challenges.answer: Sourced the Phase II report to S6 and added it as a prepared, not committed, project: it is in the post-balance-sheet review, the catalyst list and the section 7 monitoring, with a sourced reason for excluding it from the capex path (preparation stage, no final investment decision).

challenges.challenge: Section 6 says related-party transactions are "part of how the group operates" without quantifying them. The CDIA work shows a real related-party financing channel: CDIA (60% owned) holds equity-linked bonds issued by the parent and a US$238m loan receivable from CAP subsidiaries. The report instead searches the interim LK for pledged controlling shares - a disclosure that lives in the annual report/IDX filings - and reports "checked-but-not-confirmed".
challenges.answer: Quantified related-party trade flows with F27 and F28, disclosed the CDIA intra-group financing channel, and withdrew the interim-LK pledge search: the report now says pledges live in the annual report and exchange filings and flags the gap.

challenges.challenge: Net debt of US$2,478.4 treats the whole US$3,432.5m "cash" figure as cash, but the LK's cash and cash equivalents are US$2,921.3m; the other US$511.2m is "other current financial assets" - investments in non-financial institutions, bonds, listed shares and credit-linked investments at FVTPL/amortised cost (Note 10). If these are not cash-equivalent, net debt is about US$2,990m and the DCF falls roughly Rp108/share (about 7%). The report's "US$3.43bn of cash" and 3.5% cash yield rest on the same treatment.
challenges.answer: Cash is restated to the LK cash and cash equivalents (F26) through bs_cash; the separate 511.198 of other current financial assets (F30) is disclosed and carried in the bridge at 90% of fair value, with the composition stated. Report no longer calls the whole cash balance cash.

challenges.challenge: The rendered report contains repeated percentage-unit errors from applying the `pctv` format to fraction-valued placeholders: it says "Revenue grows 0.5% in FY2026E to US$10,640.0m" (the model grows 52% from 7,000.0), "the resulting EBITDA margin is 0.1%" (the model is 12.0%), "the base regime case keeps 0.3% ... the bear 0.7% ... the bull gives back -0.1%" (30%, 70%, -10%), and "terminal value at 0.5% of the total" (engine tv_share is 48.5%). A reader cannot reproduce the thesis from these lines.
challenges.answer: Replaced pctv with pct for fraction-valued placeholders: revenue_growth, ebitda_margin, tv_share and the konglo compress parameters; re-rendered and checked the percentages against the engine.

challenges.challenge: The konglo reading is described as the base case "closing 30%" of the gap, yet the resulting target of Rp1,627 is 14.4% ABOVE the Rp1,422 fundamental value, and even the bear regime case (Rp1,504) is 5.8% above it: the lens assumes the premium is kept, not closed. The same paragraph says "price sits at 1.2x our twelve-month fundamental value of Rp1,422" - Rp1,500/Rp1,422 is 1.05x; the 1.20x is price over today's fundamental value of Rp1,245.3. The HOLD's +9.0% return is a retained-premium call, not fair value, and should be said in those words.
challenges.answer: Restated the lens in correct units: price is 0.87x the twelve-month fundamental value, a discount, and the target of 1,785 sits between price and fundamental value because the lens closes only part of the discount. The old premium narrative and the 1.2x claim are removed; the embedded premium language now matches the engine.

challenges.challenge: Several citations do not say what the report claims: "the own-history multiple of 5.9x the engine derives" is the peer median (the model's own history has only P/B 10.2x and dividend yield, no EV/EBITDA); the MSCI Global Standard deletion is cited to S0 (Yahoo) rather than S9/S10; the Brent 96/84/75 deck is cited to S0 rather than the oil deck; "the group has shown it will support the price [S9]" cites the MSCI consultation, which says nothing of the sort; and "the group has a record of all four [S2, S7]" (rights, placements, spin-offs, injections) is unsupported by either source.
challenges.answer: Corrected the labels: the multiple is the peer median, not own history; the MSCI deletion is cited to S10; the Brent path is described as the house oil deck rather than S0; the unsupported claim that the group will support the price and the claim that it has used all four capital-markets routes are removed.

challenges.challenge: The effective tax rate is set at 20% against the 14.5% observed in H1-2026 (tax 62.8 on PBT 434.0) and the 22% statutory rate, with only a "normalising mix" rationale. The method card asks for the rate the LK shows being paid; on PBT of roughly US$700m the 5.5pp mark-up is about US$39m a year, roughly 2-3% of DCF value.
challenges.answer: Tax rate now starts at the observed 14.5% and steps to the 20% forecast / 22% statutory level by FY2029E, with the schedule stated in the basis.

challenges.challenge: share_change of -0.5% a year for FY2026E-FY2035E is extrapolated from a one-off buyback of up to 0.92% of shares that the company terminated early on 28 October 2026 and replaced with a new period of "different allocation" (S7). The new programme's size is unknown, so a permanent 0.5% annual shrinkage is an unsourced optimism worth roughly 2-3% of per-share value by the terminal year.
challenges.answer: Share count held flat at zero change because the replacement buyback size and term are undisclosed; the report says so explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality output contract requires the three-year accruals ratio or a specific set of flags; the report explicitly declines the Sloan ratio and gives no operating cash flow. With FY2025A np_parent of 1,090.1 but FCFF of -1,592.2, H1-2026 FCFF of -13.1 and inventories up 78% (2,237.9 from 1,254.4), cash conversion is the central quality question and is not shown.
challenges.answer: Added operating cash flow F19 and inventories F29 as facts, plus a cash-conversion discussion (operating cash flow vs EBITDA) and the working-capital scope/seasonality conclusion; the KPI list now includes operating cash flow over EBITDA.

missing_bull_case.note: Absent or understated: (i) refinery crack-spread upside in a high-Brent world - the model has no revenue-side oil term, so every oil move is a cost squeeze, and the record H1-2026 half was earned at Brent ~85; (ii) the model's own deleveraging from net debt 2,385 (FY2026E) to 1,323 (FY2028E), about 0.8x EBITDA, while section 5 says there is little headroom; (iii) Danantara/INA co-invest US$200m of the US$800m CA-EDC (S5), not reflected in capex or net debt; (iv) CDIA at its own house fundamental (Rp83 today) is worth far less than the US$704m book minority deducted; (v) related-party trade flows are tiny (RP receivables 12.993m of 844m, 1.5%), which answers the report's own governance worry.

missing_bear_case.note: Absent or understated: (i) management's "operating EBITDA" of US$802.6m is not reconciled to the LK - LK EBITDA is about US$757m (14.2%) after selling, G&A and final tax, with management adding back the US$39.1m other loss and US$7.2m associates; (ii) CA-EDC Phase II at US$1bn appears in the same S6 article but is absent from capex, scenarios and catalysts; (iii) US$511.2m of bonds/shares/credit-linked investments (Note 10) are counted as cash, flattering net debt; (iv) no debt-maturity schedule; (v) the CDIA-parent related-party financing is omitted; (vi) pledged shares were searched in the interim LK, which cannot show them; (vii) no CFO/accruals analysis.

assumption_realism.note: The three value drivers: gross margin 19.1% is a back-solve from the 16.7% actual using a 60% cost share and 80% pass-through that no source states; revenue +52% FY2026E is just annualisation of H1-2026 (5,348.8 x 2 = 10,697.6) and is fine; capex 5.5% then 4.0% tracks the 5.3% H1-2026 actual but ignores the US$1bn CA-EDC Phase II. The gross-margin driver is the binding one and rests on an uncalibrated pair.

evidence_and_citations.note: Verified: revenue 5,348.769, COGS 4,455.545, D&A 164.131, finance costs 187.867, shares 86,511.5m, CDIA 60.0%, buyback 19-28 Oct/Rp1tn/800m shares, MSCI decision 30 Jun 2027 / feedback 30 Apr 2027, OJK 7.5% to 15% with March 2027 first step, and TPIA absent from the 26 Oct HSC list. Defects: the 60%/80% key inputs are not in S2 or S6; "own-history 5.9x" is the peer median; the MSCI deletion and Brent deck are cited to S0; F2's US$1,400m is not reconciled to np_parent US$1,090.1m; and the US$1,772m bargain gain cannot be "of" a US$1,090m profit - it exceeds it.

valuation_method_fit.note: The DCF is the right primary and the cost of capital reconciles (rf 5.0%, ERP 4.2% + CRP 2.5%, beta 0.90 to 1.48, WACC 10.7%). But 25% of the blend is a Rp0 EV/EBITDA leg; the 15% PE leg capitalises the bargain-purchase gain and is called unusable yet retained; there is no NAV-at-spot or through-cycle marker statement and no cost-curve quartile, both required by the method card; the claimed CDIA "house target" equivalence is not what the bridge computes; and US$511.2m of non-cash financial assets sit in the net-debt figure.

bias_and_tone.note: The scenarios are described as mirrored and balanced, yet bull +82% (2,412) against bear -53% (624) lifts the probability-weighted value 7% above the base, and the konglo lens adds a 14% premium (1,627 vs 1,422) with every regime scenario landing above fundamental. The "fairly valued" headline understates that the +9% is a retained-premium call. The text says the forecast "holds the record half in real terms" while the model is 16-21% below the H1-2026 run-rate.
